title: Field
body:
A commutative [[Ring]] with $1 \ne 0$ in which **every non-zero element has a multiplicative
inverse**. Equivalently, and this is the way to hold it: a field is a set where all four of
$+$, $-$, $\times$, $\div$ (by anything non-zero) work and behave normally.

Two groups stacked on one set:

- $(F, +)$ is an abelian group, with identity 0
- $(F \setminus \{0\}, \times)$ is an abelian group, with identity 1
- distributivity ties them together

Removing 0 from the multiplicative group is not a technicality. $0$ has no inverse in any field,
because $0 \cdot x = 0 \ne 1$ always, which is what "you cannot divide by zero" means once it is
a theorem instead of a rule.

## The standard examples

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| $\mathbb{Q}$ | the smallest field containing $\mathbb{Z}$ |
| $\mathbb{R}$ | complete, but not algebraically closed |
| $\mathbb{C}$ | algebraically closed; every polynomial factors. See [[Complex Numbers]] |
| $\mathbb{Z}_p$, $p$ prime | finite, $p$ elements; see [[Finite Field]] |
| $F(x)$, rational functions | the fraction field of a [[Polynomial Ring]] |

Non-examples that teach something: $\mathbb{Z}$ fails because 2 has no inverse, and
$\mathbb{Z}_6$ fails because $2 \cdot 3 = 0$ makes zero divisors, which no field has.
$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime; the argument is in [[Modular Arithmetic]].

## Characteristic

The **characteristic** of $F$ is the smallest $n > 0$ with $\underbrace{1 + 1 + \cdots + 1}_{n} =
0$, and $0$ if no such $n$ exists.

**$\operatorname{char}(F)$ is either 0 or a prime.** If $n = ab$ with both factors bigger than 1,
then $(a \cdot 1)(b \cdot 1) = 0$ with neither factor zero, and a field has no zero divisors. So
a composite characteristic is impossible.

$\mathbb{Q}, \mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}$ have characteristic 0; $\mathbb{Z}_p$ has characteristic $p$.
In characteristic 2, $x + x = 0$ for every $x$, so **addition is its own inverse** and subtraction
and addition coincide. That is exactly XOR, which is why the algebra of $GF(2)$ and the algebra of
a bitwise circuit are the same subject; see [[Boolean Algebra]] and [[Finite Field]].

## Why so much of the degree assumes one

Fields are the scalars everything else is built over, and the vault leans on them constantly
without naming them:

- **[[Vector Space]]** is defined over a field. The axioms need to divide by a scalar, which is
  why $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ and not $\mathbb{Z}$.
- **Row reduction** divides by a pivot. Gaussian elimination in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] is a
  field-only algorithm, and running it over $\mathbb{Z}$ is where fractions come from.
- **[[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]]** need roots of the characteristic polynomial to exist, which
  is why $\mathbb{C}$ turns up in a first-year course: over $\mathbb{R}$ a rotation matrix simply
  has none.
- **Linear algebra over $\mathbb{Z}_2$** is what a parity check is, and it is the whole content of
  linear [[Error Correcting Code|error correcting codes]].

## The field extension story

$\mathbb{C}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ with a root of $x^2 + 1$ adjoined, which is the constructive answer
to "where does $i$ come from". That is [[Field Extension]], and it is the machinery that also
builds every [[Finite Field]] of non-prime order. [[Complex Numbers]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] takes
$\mathbb{C}$ as arithmetic and geometry, this course takes it as structure, and
[[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] takes it as analysis.
